questions.answer:
My younger cousin loves drawing. I noticed it when she visited us and asked for paper before asking for a game or a phone. She is still a child, so I wouldn't compare her drawings with professional art. What I admire is how confidently she puts an idea on the page.

She often **draws from imagination** rather than copying a picture exactly. Her drawings may have bright purple trees or houses with enormous windows, and she can always explain why each detail is there. Once she showed me a scene of a family travelling through a forest. While she described it, she **made up a whole story** about the characters. I helped her **find coloured pencils**, but she decided for herself which colours to use. When she made a mark she didn't like, she would **work it into the picture** rather than throw the page away.

I enjoy watching her because she is **not afraid of mistakes**. Adults sometimes **lose that freedom** as they become concerned with results. Her parents encourage her to **explore different materials** and praise the effort rather than demanding a perfect picture. If she keeps drawing, she may **develop her own style**. Even if she chooses another hobby later, the chance to **express her ideas** and **enjoy the process** is valuable now. She reminds me that creativity can begin with a blank page and a simple question.

Once she gave me a drawing of a city with a river running through the sky. I asked why the river was there, and she said the birds needed a road. That answer was delightful because it followed a logic of its own. I kept the picture in a folder.

questions.q: Describe a difficult decision you had to make
questions.answer:
A difficult decision I made was whether to join an extra course while I already had a demanding study schedule. The course looked useful and several friends planned to attend, so I was tempted to sign up immediately. At the same time, I knew I was struggling to finish my existing work without sacrificing sleep.

I tried to **weigh up the benefits** against the time it would take. I spoke with the teacher, looked at the timetable and **asked for honest advice** from my family. A friend pointed out that I could study the same topic independently for a while and decide later whether I needed a formal class. That gave me a **middle option** I hadn't considered. In the end I **turned down the course** for that term and used the spare hours to strengthen the subjects I was already taking.

It wasn't an exciting decision, but I felt calmer once I had made it. Had I joined simply because my friends were going, I might have **spread myself too thin**. I learned that a good opportunity can still come at the wrong time. Saying no helped me **protect my priorities** and **manage my workload**. If the course is offered again, I may reconsider when I can **give it proper attention**. For now, I am satisfied that I **made a deliberate choice** rather than allowing the fear of missing out to decide for me.

There was a moment when I almost registered anyway because the application deadline was approaching. I **slept on the decision** before choosing. That pause gave me space to separate genuine interest from the pressure of a closing date, and I have found the same habit useful in other decisions.

questions.q: Describe your ideal home
questions.answer:
I'd like to live in a modest house in a peaceful neighbourhood, ideally with plenty of light and a small garden. It doesn't need to be large or luxurious. I would rather have a place that fits everyday life well than rooms I rarely use.

The most important space would be a **quiet study corner** with a proper desk and books within reach. Large windows could **let in natural light**, while good insulation would make the rooms comfortable in different seasons. I would also like a shared area where my family could **spend time together** without everyone disappearing into separate rooms. Outside, a **small garden** would be enough for a few plants and a place to sit. I don't know exactly where this home would be; access to study or work would influence that decision.

What appeals to me is the idea of a home that **feels welcoming** rather than impressive from the street. I would try to **keep the layout simple** and avoid filling every corner with furniture. If I lived there for years, I hope it would **grow with my needs**: a room used for studying could eventually become a workspace. For me, the ideal home offers **privacy when needed**, room for guests and a **sense of belonging**. Having that balance would make it somewhere I could **settle down comfortably**.

I also hope the home would be easy to maintain. A beautiful design would become tiring if every repair required a specialist or every room was expensive to heat. Thinking about those ordinary responsibilities makes the dream more realistic, and perhaps more appealing to me.

questions.q: Describe a famous person in Uzbekistan

One day I would like to visit a museum or read a well-researched book about scholars from the region. That would help me see al-Khwarizmi within the wider intellectual world of his time. Admiration becomes more meaningful when it is followed by careful learning.

questions.q: Describe a long walk you enjoyed
questions.answer:
One long walk I enjoyed was with a friend on a cool autumn afternoon. We had planned to meet for half an hour near home, but the weather was pleasant and neither of us needed to hurry back. Without really noticing, we kept walking towards a park farther away.

We **chose a quieter route** through residential streets and stopped occasionally to look at places we normally passed without noticing. As we walked, we **caught up on each other's news** and discussed what we wanted to do after school. The conversation moved naturally from serious plans to jokes. By the time we reached the park, we had **covered more ground than expected**. We sat on a bench, shared some water and watched people walking their dogs before heading home by a different road.

I liked the walk because we had **no fixed destination**. That gave us space to **talk without rushing** and **notice our surroundings**. My legs were tired afterwards, but my mind felt lighter. If we had stayed in a noisy café, I doubt we would have talked as openly. Since then, I sometimes suggest a walk when a friend wants to discuss something important. It costs nothing, lets us **get some fresh air** and helps me **clear my head**. The experience showed me that a simple afternoon can **turn into a lasting memory** when you **make time for a friend**.

When we got back, I checked how far we had walked and was surprised by the distance. Had I set that number as a target at the start, I might have found it tiring. Because the walk grew naturally from a conversation, the effort hardly registered until we were home.

questions.q: Describe an interesting conversation with friends
questions.answer:
An interesting discussion I had with friends began after we watched a short video about using artificial intelligence in education. There were three of us, and what I expected to be a quick reaction turned into a long conversation. We all use digital tools for study, but we had different ideas about where help ends and dependence begins.

One friend argued that students should **make full use of technology** if it explains a difficult topic. Another worried that easy answers could **weaken independent thinking**. I took a middle position: a tool can help me **check my understanding**, but I still need to **work through a problem**. Rather than trying to win the argument, we **asked each other questions** about real situations, such as drafting an essay or checking a grammar mistake. Those examples helped us **move beyond general claims**.

By the end, nobody had changed their position completely, but we had **found common ground**. We agreed that students should be able to explain their own work and know when to ask a teacher. I enjoyed the discussion because everyone **listened with an open mind** and challenged ideas without making things personal. It reminded me that a useful conversation does not require a perfect answer. Sometimes its value lies in learning to **see another perspective** and **refine your own view**.

We decided to try a small experiment: each of us would solve a question independently before asking a tool for an explanation. Then we could compare our reasoning with its response. The discussion became useful because it led to a practical habit rather than ending with a slogan.

questions.q: Describe a useful invention that may change lives
questions.answer:
An invention I find especially useful is a low-cost water filter that can make drinking water safer in places where clean supplies are difficult to access. I don't have one specific brand in mind; I mean the wider idea of a durable filter that is simple to maintain. Such a device would be most valuable if people could actually afford and repair it.

The basic attraction is that it could **remove harmful particles** and help families **get access to safer water**. It might also **reduce reliance on bottled water** in some circumstances. However, a filter isn't a magic solution. People would need clear instructions, replacement parts and a way to **check that it works**. If a device broke and nobody noticed, it could create **a false sense of security**. That is why I would be more impressed by a reliable design than by a dramatic advertisement.

What makes this invention interesting to me is how a modest piece of technology can **address a basic need**. When we discuss inventions, we often think first about entertainment or convenience. Yet something that helps people **protect their health** and **save time and money** could have a greater effect. I would like engineers to **design for real conditions** and involve the communities who will use the product. If that happened, a practical water filter could **improve everyday life** for many families.

The most important test would be whether the people using it find it convenient enough to keep using. A brilliant design that takes hours to clean might sit unused in a cupboard. The social side of an invention is often just as important as the mechanism inside it.

questions.q: Describe a time you gave advice
questions.answer:
A friend once asked me how to prepare for an English speaking test. He was collecting complicated phrases but found it hard to answer a simple question without stopping. I recognised the problem because I had done something similar: I had spent too much time searching for impressive words and too little time speaking aloud.

I suggested that he **start with familiar topics** and record a short answer every day. We listened to one recording together, and I asked him to **notice where he paused** rather than judge his accent. We then practised a question twice. The second answer was more natural because he **focused on one clear idea** and added a small example. I also encouraged him to **learn phrases in context**, since memorised expressions sound odd when they do not fit the question.

I didn't promise that this would produce a particular score. Instead, I told him to **track his progress** over a few weeks and ask a teacher for **specific feedback**. A few days later he said the recordings were uncomfortable to hear but useful. That reaction made me smile, because it is how I had felt too. Giving advice taught me to **share what worked for me** without assuming everyone learns identically. The most helpful thing I did was probably to **listen first** and **keep the goal realistic**.

I **checked in with him** later, but I did not demand that he follow my plan exactly. He had adapted it to his own schedule and was practising more often. Seeing that taught me that advice works best when it gives someone a starting point, not another set of obligations.

questions.q: Describe an occasion when you had a cake
questions.answer:
An occasion I remember having a cake was a small birthday gathering at home. We didn't invite a large crowd; it was just close family and a couple of friends. I liked that scale because we could actually talk to everyone rather than spend the evening moving between tables.

One relative had **baked the cake herself**, and she kept the design simple: a little fruit on top and a short message. We **sat around the table** after dinner while someone looked for candles. When the lights went out, everybody began singing at slightly different speeds, which made us laugh. I **made a wish** and cut the cake into slices, trying to make sure the last guest got a proper piece. It tasted good, but what I remember most clearly is the **warm atmosphere** around the table.

Afterwards we **shared old stories** and looked through photographs from earlier birthdays. One picture showed us decorating a much smaller cake years before. Seeing it **brought back memories** and made me notice how quickly time had passed. The gathering wasn't expensive or elaborate, yet it **felt genuinely special**. It reminded me that a cake can be a simple excuse to **bring people together** and **celebrate another year**. If I planned another birthday, I would happily **keep it low-key** in the same way.

Before everyone went home, we saved a slice for a relative who could not attend. That gesture made the gathering feel inclusive rather than complete only for those in the room. When we brought it to them later, they were happy to hear the funny story about our uneven singing.

questions.q: Describe a school rule you like or dislike
questions.answer:
A school rule I actually appreciate is the requirement to keep phones away during lessons. It is sometimes inconvenient, particularly if I need to check a message after class, but I understand why the rule exists. In a room full of students, even one notification can interrupt more people than the owner of the phone.

Before the lesson starts, we **put our phones away** so we can **pay attention to the teacher**. That makes it easier to **follow a difficult explanation** without repeatedly losing the thread. I noticed the difference during a group task: everyone **took part in the discussion** because nobody was half-listening while scrolling. Of course, there should be **room for exceptions** if a family situation is urgent or the teacher asks us to use a device for learning.

I like the rule because it has a clear purpose rather than being a punishment for its own sake. It helps students **build a habit of focus** and shows respect for the people who are speaking. I also think it works best when teachers **explain the reason behind it** and apply it fairly. At the end of class we can **check important messages**, so we are not cut off all day. If I could improve the rule, I would make the emergency procedure clearer. Overall, it helps us **make better use of lesson time** and **avoid unnecessary distractions**.

There are days when I am tempted to glance at my phone anyway, especially if I am waiting for a reply. On those days the rule is most useful. It removes a small decision I would otherwise have to make over and over during the lesson.

questions.q: Describe an important decision you made
questions.answer:
An important decision I made was to take my English study more seriously because I hope to apply for opportunities abroad in the future. It didn't happen in one dramatic moment. I had been studying on and off, but I realised that occasional bursts of effort would not take me as far as a steady routine.

I began by **setting a long-term goal** and then asked what I could actually do each week. I chose a reading schedule, short speaking practice and time to review mistakes. At first I tried to do too much, so I had to **adjust my expectations** and **build a manageable routine**. The hardest part was continuing when progress was not obvious. I started to **keep a record of my work**, which helped me see that small efforts were adding up. I also asked teachers for **honest feedback** instead of only looking for encouragement.

The decision matters because it changed how I spend my time. I now try to **take responsibility for my learning** rather than wait for motivation to appear. I still miss a study session occasionally, and I have not achieved every goal yet. However, I have learned to **get back on track** without treating one bad day as failure. If I eventually study abroad, I will remember this as the point when I began to **turn a vague hope into a plan**. Even if my destination changes, the ability to **make deliberate choices** and **follow through** will remain useful.

I sometimes compare my current ability with where I hoped to be and feel impatient. Then I look back at something I wrote months ago and notice progress I missed day to day. That perspective helps me keep the decision sustainable rather than turning it into constant pressure.

part2.title: Home you like but would not live in

questions.q: Describe a friend's home you like but would not choose for yourself
questions.answer:
A friend's apartment is a place I enjoy visiting but would not choose as my long-term home. It is on an upper floor of a modern building, with a broad view over the city. The first time I walked in, the sunlight and open layout made it feel much bigger than I had expected.

My friend has **made good use of the space**. A desk sits beside the window, plants add colour and the main room is comfortable enough for several friends to sit and talk. I particularly like how the windows **let in natural light** and how everything has **a place of its own**. When we study there, it is easy to **settle down to work**. Afterwards, we sometimes make tea and look out over the streets below.

Still, I would not want to **live there permanently**. The building is close to a busy road, so traffic is audible even with the windows shut. Reaching the apartment also depends on a lift, and I would miss having a small outdoor area. For a visit, those things hardly matter; for everyday life, they might. If I had to choose, I would prefer a quieter house where I could **step outside easily** and perhaps **grow a few plants**. I can **appreciate the design** and **enjoy the view** while recognising that it does not **suit my daily routine**. My friend loves it, which is a good reminder that a home must fit the person who lives there.

I once stayed there for an entire afternoon while we prepared a school task. By evening the road noise was far more noticeable than it had been when I arrived. That visit helped me distinguish between a place that photographs well and one that would feel restful every day.

questions.q: Describe a famous person you have seen in the news
questions.answer:
A famous person I remember seeing in the news is the tennis player Novak Djokovic. The story I saw was about a major tournament result, but I would rather focus on why it caught my attention than risk mixing up the score or the date. I don't follow every match; I recognised him because of his long career and the pressure that comes with competing at the highest level.

The report showed a few points and then an interview. What interested me was the contrast between the **public celebration** and the calm way he **answered difficult questions**. A few minutes of highlights can make a result look inevitable, whereas a match involves **countless small decisions**. I wondered how a sportsperson **handles expectations** when so many people comment on every performance. The news also made me think about how easy it is for a viewer to **judge from a distance** without knowing the work or setbacks behind the result.

I don't know him personally, so I cannot claim to understand his character. Still, the story reminded me that success often requires the ability to **recover from mistakes** and **stay focused under pressure**. If I wanted a fuller picture, I would **look beyond the headline** and read a reliable account of the whole match. What I took away was less a lesson about tennis than a reminder to **respect sustained effort** and **avoid quick conclusions**.

The report was brief, so it gave me an impression rather than a full understanding of the event. I would be reluctant to use it to judge a player's entire career. An individual story becomes more interesting when I consider what I do not know as well as what the camera shows.

questions.q: Describe a letter, email or message you wrote to someone living far away
questions.answer:
Last year I wrote a long message to a relative living in another city. We usually exchange short greetings, but she had asked how my studies were going, and I wanted to give a proper answer. I typed it on my phone one evening, then read it again before sending it because I did not want it to sound like a list of achievements.

I began by **asking how she was doing** and mentioning a family event she had missed. Then I **gave her an update** about my English practice and a small website I was trying to build. I included one difficulty too: I had been struggling to **keep a consistent routine**. She had supported me before, so it felt natural to be honest rather than pretend everything was effortless. I also sent a photograph of a place we had visited together, hoping it would **bring back a good memory**.

She replied the next day with a thoughtful message of her own. Instead of giving me a lecture, she **shared a practical suggestion** about dividing a large goal into smaller steps. Our exchange helped us **stay connected across the distance**. A phone call might have been quicker, but writing allowed me to **choose my words carefully** and let her respond when she had time. I still have the conversation saved. It reminds me that a personal message can **mean a great deal** when you **make time for someone** and **write with genuine interest**.

She later said she appreciated the photograph most because it reminded her of being with the family. I had spent more time writing about study, but that small image connected the message to a shared experience. Since then, I try to include one personal detail when I write to someone far away.

questions.q: Describe an interview with a well-known person you saw or heard
questions.answer:
An interview that stayed with me was a recorded conversation with an astronaut about living and working in space. I found it while watching educational videos, and the questions were more practical than I had expected. Instead of asking only how spectacular the view was, the interviewer asked about ordinary routines and mistakes.

The astronaut described how a team has to **follow precise procedures** while still being able to **respond to unexpected problems**. One answer concerned a task that had taken much longer than planned. I liked that she **admitted the difficulty** rather than presenting the work as effortless. The interviewer then **asked a follow-up question** about how the crew communicated, which brought out a much more useful answer than a simple yes or no. I paused the recording a few times to **take in the details**.

What made the interview engaging was the balance between expertise and an ordinary human voice. I could **picture the situation** without pretending that I had experienced it myself. It also showed me how a good interviewer can **draw out a story** by listening rather than rushing to the next question. If I were able to ask the astronaut something, I would ask how that experience changed her view of teamwork back on Earth. The interview encouraged me to **ask better questions** and **look past dramatic headlines**. Even now, I remember the calm way she explained a demanding job.

I also noticed that the interviewer let her finish an answer even when she paused to think. That patience **made the conversation feel natural** and allowed an unexpected detail to emerge. Had every answer been cut short, I probably would not remember the interview as clearly.

questions.q: Describe a speech or conversation that did not interest you
questions.answer:
I once attended a long talk at a school event about a topic I had initially expected to enjoy: planning future careers. The speaker clearly had experience, so I do not want to dismiss the subject or the person. The problem was that the talk consisted mostly of broad advice with very few examples, and the audience had little chance to ask questions.

During the first ten minutes I tried to **follow the main argument**. Then the same points began to **come up repeatedly**, and I found myself **losing concentration**. I still **listened politely** because leaving in the middle would have been disruptive. To stay engaged, I wrote down two questions I would have liked to ask: how a student might **explore a field practically** and how to decide between competing interests. Neither was addressed directly.

The experience made me realise that a valuable topic does not automatically make an interesting presentation. The speaker might have **held our attention** with a short story, a case study or time for discussion. I also learned something about myself: when I give a presentation, I should **respect the audience's time**, **use concrete examples** and avoid repeating a point simply to fill the allotted time. Although I was bored, I tried not to **judge the speaker harshly**, because public speaking is difficult. That afternoon gave me a clearer idea of how to make my own explanations more useful.

Afterwards a friend asked what I thought of the talk, and I described the parts that had not answered my questions without mocking the speaker. That helped us **give fair criticism**. I would still attend another talk on the same subject if it offered concrete examples and space for questions.

questions.q: Describe an interesting place you visited on vacation
questions.answer:
On a family holiday in Samarkand, we visited a small craft workshop away from the busiest tourist area. It was not the main place on our itinerary; we went in because we saw someone working near the entrance and became curious. That unplanned visit became one of the details I remember most vividly.

Inside, an artisan showed us part of the process of making a decorative object. I was surprised by how many stages were involved before the finished piece could be **put on display**. She let us **look closely at the tools** and explained how one small mistake could change a pattern. I had expected to **browse the shelves** for five minutes, but we stayed much longer and **asked plenty of questions**. My younger relative noticed a colour combination that I had overlooked, and we ended up discussing it on the way back.

The workshop gave me a different impression of the city. Famous buildings are memorable, but meeting someone who **practises a craft** helped me **see the work behind an object**. We did not buy much; the value of the visit was the conversation and the chance to observe. If I went again, I would **set aside more time** for similar small places. They can **offer a fresh perspective** on a destination and **turn an ordinary afternoon into a memory**.

Before we left, I looked again at the finished objects and noticed details I had not seen on arrival. Understanding even a little of the process **changed the way I looked at them**. That is why I consider the workshop an interesting holiday stop rather than just a shop.

questions.q: Describe an event you really enjoyed
questions.answer:
One event I enjoyed was a reading afternoon organised by a small local bookshop. It was modest compared with a concert or a festival: perhaps a dozen people gathered to discuss a short story. I almost did not go because I thought I would have nothing interesting to say, but a friend persuaded me to join him.

At the beginning, the organiser **put everyone at ease** by asking which part of the story had surprised us. That was easier to answer than a formal literary question. I **shared my first impression**, then listened as others **offered different interpretations**. One person had noticed a detail about the ending that I had missed entirely. The discussion was lively without becoming competitive, and afterwards we **stayed for tea**. I spoke to someone who had started reading in English only recently, which reminded me how varied people's reasons for joining can be.

I enjoyed the event because it made a solitary activity feel social. It gave me a reason to **read more carefully** and the confidence to **speak up in a group**. Had I stayed home, I would probably have forgotten the story within a week. Instead, the conversation **brought it to life** and helped me **connect with other readers**. I would go to a similar event again, especially if it kept the same **welcoming atmosphere**.

The organiser also asked quieter people for their views without putting them under pressure. That **made the discussion inclusive** and prevented a few confident voices from dominating. I left thinking that a small event can be memorable when everyone feels welcome to contribute.

questions.q: Describe someone who makes things by hand or with technology
questions.answer:
A friend of mine enjoys making useful things from simple materials and experimenting with digital tools. His projects are small, but each one solves a real problem for someone he knows. I first noticed his skill when he made an adjustable book stand for his younger brother, who found it uncomfortable to study with a book lying flat on the desk.

He began by **sketching a rough design** on paper, then **measured the pieces carefully**. The first version wobbled, so he changed the angle and reinforced the base. He also used a simple computer program to **test different dimensions** before cutting new material. Watching him work, I was impressed by his willingness to **learn through trial and error**. When the stand was finally stable, he asked his brother to use it for a week and **give honest feedback**. Only then did he call the project finished.

What I admire is his ability to **turn an idea into something practical**. He doesn't pretend that every attempt succeeds, and he is happy to **start from scratch** if a design is flawed. I think that combination of patience and curiosity is more valuable than simply owning expensive equipment. He has encouraged me to **solve everyday problems creatively** and to **pay attention to the user**. If I were building something with him, I would want to learn how he decides when a product is **good enough to use**.

He later made a second stand for a friend, changing the width to fit a larger book. That showed me he was not simply repeating a design; he was listening to a different user's needs. The project was modest, but it reflected a thoughtful way of working.

It did not rely on a famous person; instead, it showed a student trying to practise speaking while everyone around him was busy. The scenes were short and the message was easy to follow: you could **practise in small moments** rather than wait for an ideal hour. I liked the **clear visual storytelling** and the way it **avoided complicated claims**. Still, I noticed that it did not explain how the app gives feedback or whether a real teacher is involved. Those details would matter to me more than the cheerful ending.

I didn't download it straight away. I **checked independent reviews** and looked at what the free version actually offered. The advert had successfully **sparked my interest**, but interest is different from trust. Even though I chose a different way to practise, I still remember the central idea: **consistent practice** matters more than a perfect setting. That makes it a good advert in my view, even if I did not become a customer.

The ad's strongest feature was that the learner's progress looked gradual. It did not show him becoming fluent overnight. questions.q: Describe a food you dislike
questions.answer:
One food I have never really enjoyed is an overly sweet fruit dessert with heavy syrup. I do not dislike fruit itself; in fact, I often eat it fresh. It is the combination of the thick syrup and a very soft texture that puts me off. I first tried the dessert at a family gathering, where everyone else seemed to enjoy it.

I took a small portion because I wanted to **give it a fair chance**. The first bite was much sweeter than I expected, and after a few mouthfuls I **lost my appetite for it**. I did not make a dramatic comment, since someone had spent time preparing it. I thanked the host and chose a little tea instead. Later, when my family asked why I had left some, I explained that I **prefer lighter flavours** and usually like fruit without additional syrup.

I am aware that **taste is personal**. My relative loves that dessert, and I would never claim it is badly made simply because it does not suit me. If it were prepared with less syrup, I might **try it again**. Until then, I would rather **choose a different dessert** or have fruit on its own. The experience taught me to **be polite about food** when someone offers it, while still being honest about my preferences. I think you can **decline a second serving** without embarrassing the cook. For me, a meal is about company as well as flavour, so I would not let one disliked dish **spoil the occasion**.

I have tried other versions of the dessert, and my reaction was similar. I can still appreciate the care involved in serving it and enjoy the rest of the meal. **Respecting other people's tastes** matters to me.

questions.q: Describe a place in nature you like
questions.answer:
There is a stretch of countryside near relatives' home that I enjoy visiting when I have the chance. It is not a famous protected area or a dramatic mountain landscape. There are fields, a line of trees and a footpath that becomes particularly pleasant in the late afternoon.

On my last visit I went there with a relative after breakfast. We **followed a narrow path** and gradually left the sound of traffic behind. I could **hear birds calling** and see how the light changed over the crops. My relative pointed out where rain had changed the soil, a detail I would have missed on my own. We stopped for a while to **take in the view** and then walked back before the day became too hot. Nothing dramatic happened, but I felt calmer for having spent time there.

What I value is the chance to **slow my pace** and **pay attention to small changes**. On a screen I often move quickly from one thing to another; outdoors, I can **clear my head** without trying to be productive. I also know the area is part of people's working lives, so I try to **respect the land** and **leave no litter behind**. If I lived nearby, I would **visit more regularly**. Even an ordinary landscape can **leave a lasting impression** when you have time to notice it.

On that walk I also noticed a small change in the weather before my relative mentioned it. The air became cooler and the light softened. Those are details I would probably miss if I were rushing to reach a landmark. The place rewards attention rather than a packed itinerary.

questions.q: Describe a journey you often make but dislike
questions.answer:
A journey I often make but do not enjoy is a crowded bus ride to a learning centre during the busiest part of the day. Most trips are perfectly manageable, and I am grateful there is a route at all. The problem is the combination of traffic, noise and uncertainty about how long the journey will take.

One afternoon stands out. I had allowed what I thought was plenty of time, but a delay meant the bus **moved at a crawl** for much of the route. The vehicle was full, so it was difficult to **find a comfortable place to stand**. I kept **checking the time**, worrying that I would miss the start of a class. When we finally got moving, the noise made it hard to concentrate on the notes I had brought. I arrived just in time, but I felt tired before the lesson had even begun.

Since then, I have tried to **leave a little earlier** and **prepare a backup route** when something important is scheduled. I also avoid expecting myself to study seriously on a crowded bus; listening to a short recording is more realistic. The journey is not a disaster, but it can **put me in a bad mood** if I let every delay frustrate me. Ideally, more predictable transport would **make daily life easier** for everyone using the route. For now, I try to **plan around the uncertainty** and **arrive with time to spare**.

One day I considered walking the last section instead of staying on the bus, but it would have taken too long before class. The experience helped me **make more realistic plans**: a route may look short on a map and still be unpredictable at a busy hour.

questions.q: Describe someone who struggled but succeeded
questions.answer:
A person I admire is an older acquaintance who had to rebuild his small tutoring business after an unexpectedly difficult year. I do not know every financial detail, so I would not present his story as a business case study. What I saw was the effort he made to keep serving students when his first plan stopped working.

He had relied mainly on in-person lessons, but circumstances changed and attendance fell. Rather than **give up on the project**, he asked students what they needed and **adapted his teaching materials**. He began with short online sessions, discovered that some students had poor connections and then created smaller downloadable exercises. He also **asked for honest feedback** instead of pretending that every change was successful. For a while he seemed exhausted, but he continued to **make steady improvements**. Gradually students returned, and his lessons became more flexible than before.

What I respect is his **willingness to change course**. Success did not come from a single brilliant idea; it came from noticing problems and responding to them. He told me once that he had learned to **take one step at a time** when the bigger picture felt overwhelming. Watching him encouraged me to **deal with setbacks** without treating them as a verdict on my ability. I cannot say his work is easy now, but he has **regained his confidence** and **kept his commitment to students**. That is the kind of success I find convincing.

I once asked him whether he wished he had started with a different plan. He said the first version had taught him what students really needed, even though it failed in some ways. That answer helped me **see failure as information** rather than just an embarrassing outcome.

questions.q: Describe someone interested in becoming a doctor or nurse
questions.answer:
A school friend of mine hopes to work in medicine, ideally as a doctor. We have known each other for several years, and I have seen how seriously she takes biology. She is also the person in our group who listens carefully when someone is worried, although I know that kindness alone is not enough for a medical career.

She first **became interested in healthcare** after accompanying a family member to a clinic. What stayed with her was how a clinician **explained each step clearly**, making a stressful visit easier to handle. Since then, my friend has **worked hard at science** and looked into the years of training involved. She knows she will have to **develop practical skills** as well as pass examinations. When we discuss the future, she speaks about caring for patients, but also about the need to **make careful decisions** when information is incomplete.

I admire her because she does not **romanticise the profession**. She understands that long hours and difficult conversations may be part of the job. If she eventually qualifies, I think her ability to **treat people with respect** will matter alongside medical knowledge. I cannot predict exactly where her studies will lead, but she is willing to **put in sustained effort**. Talking with her has reminded me that choosing a profession means learning about its **everyday responsibilities**, not only its title. I hope she gets the chance to **follow that path**.

She sometimes asks me to listen while she explains a science concept in plain language. It helps her check what she understands, and I often learn something too. I like that she shares what she learns rather than treating study as a private competition.

questions.q: Describe a time you received good service
questions.answer:
I once received excellent service in a small bookshop when I was looking for an English book that would challenge me without being frustrating. I had been browsing for a while, and a member of staff asked whether I wanted a suggestion. She did not immediately direct me to the most expensive shelf.

First she **asked about my reading level** and what kind of subjects I enjoyed. I explained that I wanted a story with language I could follow but also learn from. She showed me two options and **pointed out the differences** in length and style. Then she suggested that I **read a page from each** before deciding. That simple idea helped me notice that one book felt manageable and the other required a dictionary in almost every paragraph. She gave me time to **make up my own mind** and never made me feel rushed.

I bought the first book and later returned to thank her because I actually finished it. What made the service good was her willingness to **listen to my needs** rather than assume what I should buy. She had **offered useful guidance** without pressuring me. I left with a book that helped me **build my reading confidence** and a more positive impression of the shop. If I owned a business, I would want customers to **feel comfortable asking questions** and to know that staff **care about the right fit**.

The next time I entered the shop, the same staff member recognised the title and asked whether it had been a suitable choice. That follow-up **made the service feel personal**, even though our conversation was brief. It gave me confidence to ask for another recommendation when I was ready.

questions.q: Describe a time you saw children misbehaving
questions.answer:
I remember seeing a group of children behaving badly on a bus one afternoon. They were not doing anything dangerous, but they were shouting across the aisle and repeatedly kicking the back of another passenger's seat. The adult travelling with them seemed distracted and did not notice at first.

I initially tried to **ignore the noise**, because children can get restless on a long journey. Then the passenger in front turned round and **asked them politely** to stop kicking the seat. The children laughed, and one of them carried on. Their adult companion finally noticed and **spoke to them firmly**. She did not shout, but she explained that other people needed space too. After a few minutes they settled down, and the passenger thanked her. Watching the situation, I realised how easy it would be to **make a snap judgement** about the family without knowing whether the children were tired or upset.

The behaviour was inconsiderate, yet I think the calm response worked better than public humiliation would have. Children have to **learn social boundaries**, and adults can help by **setting clear expectations**. If I had been the passenger, I hope I could have **raised the issue respectfully**. The incident made me think about how shared spaces depend on people **taking others into account**. It also reminded me that correcting behaviour does not require **losing your temper** or **embarrassing a child**.

I also noticed that the children settled more quickly once the adult gave them something to do during the rest of the journey. That small change suggested they had been restless, not deliberately trying to upset strangers. It did not excuse the kicking, but it made the situation easier to understand.

questions.q: Describe a problem you helped someone with
questions.answer:
A friend once asked for help because he could not open a presentation file on the computer at our learning centre. We were due to present in less than an hour. He had prepared the slides at home, so losing access to them at that moment felt serious.

I suggested we **check the file format** before making random changes. It turned out that the centre's computer did not have the same presentation software he had used. We tried opening the file in a browser, but a few images moved out of place. Instead of spending all our time **fixing every small detail**, we **focused on the essential slides** and saved a simpler version as a PDF. I also asked him to **keep a backup copy** on his phone. We rehearsed the opening together while the document was loading, which helped him calm down.

The presentation went ahead, and most of the audience never knew there had been a problem. My friend thanked me afterwards, although he had done the main work himself. What I contributed was a way to **break the problem down** and **make a practical choice** under time pressure. Since then, I have tested my own files on another device before an event. The experience showed me that helping someone does not always mean having advanced technical knowledge; sometimes it means **staying calm**, **asking the right questions** and **working together on a solution**.

Before the next presentation, my friend saved a PDF from the start. He said the incident had been stressful but useful because it changed his preparation. I was glad the solution had **held up under pressure**, but even more glad we had both learned a habit we could use again.

questions.q: Describe something you saved up for
questions.answer:
I once saved money to buy a pair of reliable headphones for English listening practice. My old pair had an uneven sound, and I was tired of missing words during podcasts. I could have asked my family to buy a replacement immediately, but I wanted to contribute and choose carefully.

I began by **setting a clear budget** and putting aside a small amount of money when I could. I **compared several models** and read reviews about comfort rather than focusing only on appearance. A friend suggested a more expensive pair, but it cost more than I could sensibly spend. I waited a little longer, then found a suitable option at a fair price. Before paying, I **tested the sound quality** and checked whether the fit would be comfortable for a longer study session. I also kept my receipt in case there was a problem.

Saving for it made the purchase feel more deliberate. I had to **resist small impulse purchases**, and that helped me see how quickly little expenses add up. When I finally used the headphones for a listening lesson, I could **hear the recording clearly** without turning the volume too high. I told a close friend what I was saving for, and he occasionally asked how it was going, but I did not make a big announcement. The experience taught me to **plan ahead financially**, **choose for my needs** and **appreciate what I buy**.

It took several weeks to reach my target, so I had time to **reconsider the purchase**. Once I was still sure I needed it, I felt comfortable spending the money. I did not tell many people about the plan; I **kept it fairly private** until I had chosen a pair.

questions.q: Describe a noisy place you have been to
questions.answer:
One of the noisiest places I remember visiting was a crowded indoor market before a holiday. My family needed a few things, so I went along to help carry the bags. I expected it to be busy, but the sound was much more intense than I had imagined.

Traders were **calling out their prices**, customers were talking over one another, and music from several stalls blended into the background. I found it hard to **hear the person next to me**, so we agreed to stay close and meet by a particular entrance if we became separated. At one point I stepped aside to **get my bearings**. I noticed that the market had its own rhythm: as soon as a customer left one counter, another took their place. We bought what we needed fairly quickly, but by the time we came out, my head felt full.

I can understand why some people enjoy that **lively atmosphere**. It gives the place energy and makes shopping feel social. For me, though, the constant noise made it difficult to **think clearly** and **compare prices calmly**. If I went back, I would try to **visit at a quieter time** and bring a short list. The experience reminded me that what feels exciting to one person can be exhausting to another. I was relieved to **step outside into fresh air** and **enjoy a moment of quiet** before heading home.

When we reached a quieter street, I noticed I was speaking louder than necessary because I had adjusted to the market. That made me laugh, but it also showed how strongly the environment had affected us. The contrast helped me **appreciate the silence** on the way home.

questions.q: Describe an enjoyable evening spent with friends
questions.answer:
An evening I particularly enjoyed was a small gathering at a friend's home after we had finished a set of exams. There were four of us, and we deliberately kept the plan simple. Everyone brought a snack, and our host chose a film we had all wanted to watch.

We arrived just before sunset and **helped set the table**. Before starting the film, we **caught up on each other's news** because we had been too busy to talk properly for weeks. Halfway through, someone paused it to ask a question about the plot, and that turned into a funny debate about what the main character should do. We eventually finished watching, then played a short game that made everyone **burst out laughing**. The evening did not cost much; its appeal was the relaxed company.

I liked how we could **let our guard down** after a demanding period. There was no strict schedule or pressure to make the night impressive. We **shared a simple meal** and talked until it was time to go home. Looking back, I remember the conversation more clearly than the film. It was a chance to **reconnect with friends** and **celebrate a small milestone**. If I organised another evening like it, I would keep the same idea: **make room for conversation** and let the rest happen naturally. Those ordinary moments can **turn into lasting memories**.

One friend had been especially worried about the exam, so it was good to see him relax. We did not spend the whole night discussing results; after a while, the subject simply faded. That shift **made the evening feel like a break** rather than an extension of our study week.

questions.q: Describe a sports event you watched and enjoyed
questions.answer:
I once watched a local football match with a friend, and the atmosphere was far more engaging than watching a recording at home. Neither of us had a strong connection to either team. We went because we wanted to see a live game and spend an afternoon together.

The first half was fairly quiet, but the pace changed after a team **created a good chance** and narrowly missed. From our seats, we could hear players **calling to one another** and see how quickly they **adjusted their positions**. A player on the other side of the field scored later, and the crowd **erupted in cheers**. I was surprised by how much the shared reaction affected me, even though I hadn't arrived supporting that team. The match stayed close until the end, so people around us were **watching every move**.

What I liked most was the **sense of anticipation** between important moments. On a screen, I can replay a goal, but in the stadium I had to **pay attention in real time**. Afterwards my friend and I talked about a decision the referee had made, though neither of us pretended to know all the rules perfectly. I left appreciating the players' **teamwork under pressure** and the energy of the spectators. I would **go to another live match** if I had the chance, especially with someone who enjoys discussing the game afterwards.

On the way home, I realised I could remember individual passes that would have disappeared into a highlight reel. The slow periods had helped build the tension. Being there **changed my view of live sport**: the atmosphere and anticipation were as important as the final score.

questions.q: Describe something you do regularly but consider a waste of time
questions.answer:
A routine I consider a waste of time is checking several apps in a row when I am about to start studying. I tell myself I am only looking for an important message, but one notification leads to another. Ten minutes can pass before I have opened the book I intended to read.

I first noticed the habit when I **tracked my study sessions**. The problem was not any single app; it was the repeated decision to **pick up my phone** whenever a task felt difficult. If I didn't immediately understand a paragraph, I would **look for an easy distraction** rather than work through it. The routine gave me a false sense of being busy, even though I rarely **found anything urgent**. Once I saw the pattern, I began to **turn off notifications** and leave the phone out of reach for a short block of time.

I still need my phone for study sometimes, so simply banning it would be unrealistic. What helps is **setting a specific purpose** before I unlock it: am I checking a word or just avoiding an awkward question? If it is the latter, I try to **return to the task** for five minutes. That small change has helped me **protect my attention** without pretending I will never use social media. I would rather **make conscious choices** than let an automatic routine **eat into my time**.

I now put a piece of paper next to my desk and write down any unrelated thought that occurs while I work. That keeps me from opening an app to deal with it immediately. At the end of a study block, I can decide whether the thought was actually important.

questions.q: Describe a place connected to an event you attended
questions.answer:
The place I would describe is a small community hall where our learning centre held a student presentation evening. From outside it looked quite plain. Inside, however, the organisers had arranged the chairs in a semicircle, which made the room feel more welcoming than a traditional stage setup.

I arrived early to help **set up the equipment** and check whether everyone could see the screen. As guests came in, the hall **filled with conversation**. Students were nervous about presenting, but the semicircle made it easier to **make eye contact** with familiar faces. During one talk, a student accidentally skipped a slide. Instead of panicking, she explained the point in her own words, and the audience **gave her a warm response**. After the presentations, we moved the chairs aside and **shared tea and snacks**.

The event changed how I saw the hall. Had I passed it on an ordinary day, I might not have noticed it. Because of what happened there, it now **brings back memories** of people encouraging one another. The building was not luxurious, but it **served its purpose well**: everyone could hear, participate and stay to talk afterwards. If I planned another event, I would choose a venue that **puts people at ease** rather than one that merely looks impressive. The evening showed me that a place gains meaning from the **shared experience** inside it.

A few students had been reluctant to present, so the organisers allowed them to practise in the empty hall first. When I learned that later, the confident performances made more sense. A comfortable venue did not remove their nerves, but it **gave them a fair chance** to show their work.

questions.q: Describe a neighbour you find interesting
questions.answer:
One neighbour I find interesting is an older man who repairs bicycles as a hobby. I have known him by sight for years, but we began talking when the chain on my cousin's bicycle came loose. He offered to take a look and explained what he was doing rather than simply fixing it in silence.

His small workbench is always **neatly organised**. He has a habit of **keeping old parts** and finding a new use for them when something breaks. While he worked on the bicycle, he told us about how transport in the neighbourhood had changed since he was young. I liked the way he **connected everyday objects with stories**. He didn't claim to know everything: when he was unsure whether one part would fit, he measured it and **checked before replacing it**. The bicycle was ready by the next afternoon, and my cousin was delighted.

What makes him interesting to me is his combination of practical skill and patience. He **takes time to explain** things to younger neighbours, even when there is no reason for him to do so. I have learned to **ask better questions** when I see him working. Our conversations are usually brief, but they create a **friendly connection** in the area. If I ever have the chance, I would like to **learn a basic repair** from him. Knowing someone like that nearby makes the neighbourhood **feel more like a community**, rather than just a collection of houses.

He once told me he enjoys fixing a bicycle more when the owner learns how to maintain it afterwards. That attitude **sets him apart** from someone who merely wants to show how skilled he is. It also explains why young neighbours feel comfortable asking him for help.

questions.answer:
A building I like visiting is a public library in a nearby city. I first went there with a friend while looking for a quiet place to study. From the street it looked fairly ordinary, but inside it had high windows, clear signs and several different spaces for reading or working together.

I like to **find a seat by the window** and work for an hour before walking around the shelves. The room has a **calm atmosphere** without feeling unfriendly. On my first visit, a staff member **showed us where to go** and explained which tables were for group work. That mattered because we could **speak quietly together** without disturbing someone reading alone. There were books I had not expected to find, and I left with a list of titles to look up later.

The building is attractive to me because its design **makes studying easier**. Natural light and clear directions are simple features, yet they change how long I can concentrate. I also enjoy seeing people of different ages **make use of a shared space**. Whenever I visit, I feel a gentle pressure to **put my phone away** and **focus on my work**. If I could improve one thing, I would add a few more desks at busy times. Overall, it is a place where I can **learn something new** and leave feeling that my time was well spent.

I like that visiting costs nothing, which makes the library available even when I do not plan to buy a book or a drink. It is one of the few buildings where I can stay for a while without feeling that I must spend money. That openness **adds to its appeal**.

questions.answer:
A shop I visit fairly often is a small bookshop near a road I use on the way to class. It sells books, notebooks and a few everyday study supplies. I don't buy something on every visit; sometimes I just look at the new titles and make a note of what I might want to read later.

The owner has **arranged the shelves clearly**, so it is easy to **find a particular section**. I usually browse the English-learning books first, then look at the stationery. Once I asked for a book at a suitable level, and the owner **offered a helpful suggestion** without trying to sell me the most expensive option. I appreciated that she **took my budget into account**. I bought the book and returned after finishing it to see what else she would recommend.

I like the shop because it feels personal and easy to use. The staff **remember regular customers** but never make me feel obliged to spend money. If I am planning to buy something, I still **compare prices** and think about whether I need it. But I enjoy **supporting a local business** when the service is good. The place has become part of my weekly routine: a short visit helps me **discover new books** and **stay curious about reading**, even during busy study periods.

questions.q: Describe a time you changed your mind about something
questions.answer:
I changed my opinion about studying with other people. For a long time I assumed group study was mostly a chance to talk and lose focus. I preferred working alone and avoided invitations to revise with classmates. Then I joined a small group before an English exam because I was struggling with one part of the reading section.

We **agreed on a clear goal**: each of us would try a short passage independently, then explain the questions we had answered differently. That structure prevented the meeting from becoming casual conversation. When I explained my choice, a classmate **pointed out a clue** I had missed in the text. In return, I helped another student understand why a similar-looking phrase did not support her answer. We **learned from each other's mistakes** and finished the session with a clearer idea of what to practise next.

I did not suddenly decide that every group is effective. Without a goal, a study session can still **drift off topic**. But that experience made me **reconsider my assumption**. I now study alone when I need quiet concentration and **work with others** when discussion can reveal something I have overlooked. Changing my mind felt slightly uncomfortable because I had been so certain. In the end, I was glad I had **given it a fair try**. It taught me to **stay open to evidence** and **avoid judging too quickly**.

I have since used the same approach with another assumption: I first ask what evidence might change my view. That does not mean I abandon my opinion whenever someone disagrees. It means I can **test an idea fairly** rather than protect it automatically.

questions.q: Describe an occasion when you got up very early
questions.answer:
One morning I got up much earlier than usual to travel with my family to Samarkand. We wanted to arrive with enough time to enjoy the day without rushing from place to place. My alarm went off while it was still dark, and for a moment I wondered why I had agreed to the plan.

I **got ready in silence** so I would not wake anyone who was still sleeping. We **set off before sunrise** with a simple breakfast packed for the journey. At first I was sleepy, but watching the sky become brighter through the window gradually **lifted my mood**. There were fewer vehicles on the road, and we could **travel at a steady pace**. By the time we arrived, the city was becoming busy and we had almost the whole day ahead of us.

Getting up early was worth it because it gave us **more time to explore**. We could stop for tea and **take our time** rather than constantly check a schedule. I did feel tired later in the afternoon, so I would not make a habit of sleeping too little. Had we left several hours later, we might have spent more of the trip worrying about what to miss. The experience showed me that an early start can **make a day feel longer** when it is planned sensibly. I went to bed early that evening with **vivid memories** of the journey.

I remember stopping for a quick breakfast after arriving and feeling pleased that we were not already behind schedule. The early start had **taken some pressure off**. If I repeated the trip, I would still prepare the night before so the morning remained calm. I would also **make time to rest** later.

questions.q: Describe an athlete who performed well in an important event
questions.answer:
A sportsperson whose performance impressed me is a young player I watched in a local football final. I do not know his name well enough to give a full biography, and the match was not a national event. What stayed with me was how he behaved when his team was under pressure.

In the first half he missed a good chance, and the crowd reacted loudly. For a moment he looked disappointed, but he **got back into the game** and continued to **support his teammates**. Later, when the other team pressed forward, he made a careful pass that **created an opening**. A teammate scored from the move. I was impressed that he did not **try to take all the credit** afterwards; he pointed to the team and the work they had done in training. The final minutes were tense, but they **held on to their lead**.

I call his performance successful because it involved more than one good moment. He **recovered from a mistake**, **made a smart decision under pressure** and helped others play well. I cannot know how he felt inside, but from the stands he appeared determined rather than panicked. The event reminded me that an important performance is rarely perfect. What counts is whether you can **stay involved** when something goes wrong and **contribute to a shared result**. I left the match admiring his attitude as much as his skill.

A younger player nearby watched him after the missed chance and applauded when he made the decisive pass. That response stayed with me. The athlete had **set an example** by continuing to contribute when it would have been easy to dwell on one error.

questions.q: Describe a health-related article you read
questions.answer:
I read an article about how poor sleep can affect concentration in teenagers. I found it while looking for ways to organise my study routine, since I had noticed that staying up late made difficult reading passages feel even harder the next day. The article was written for a general audience, not as personal medical advice, and I read it with that distinction in mind.

It discussed the link between sleep and attention and suggested **keeping a regular schedule**. I liked that it **explained the reasoning** rather than offering a dramatic shortcut. At the same time, I **checked the source** because online health claims can sound confident even when they are weakly supported. I also noticed that the piece did not pretend every tired student has the same problem. If someone has persistent symptoms, a general article cannot **replace professional advice**.

What I took from the article was a practical question: was I **giving myself enough time to sleep** before blaming my concentration on a difficult subject? For a week I tried to **put my phone away earlier** and **notice the difference**. That small experiment did not answer every question about health, but it helped me **pay attention to my habits**. I would recommend reading such articles critically, **avoiding sweeping claims** and **asking for help when needed**.

I would be careful not to draw a medical conclusion from my own one-week experiment. The article helped me ask better questions about my routine; it did not diagnose a condition. For any ongoing difficulty, I would seek qualified guidance rather than rely on a single webpage.

questions.q: Describe a time you collaborated on a project
questions.answer:
I once worked with two classmates on a short presentation about reducing waste at school. We were given a week and had to explain one practical change rather than list every environmental problem. At first we had different ideas: one person wanted posters, another wanted more bins, and I wanted to focus on how students could find clear information.

We **divided the work fairly** after agreeing on a shared aim. I drafted the outline, one classmate gathered examples and the other prepared the slides. Halfway through, we realised that our presentation had become too broad. We **cut less relevant points** and **built a clearer argument** around labelled collection points and simple instructions. We then **rehearsed together** so the transitions between speakers would feel natural. When one slide failed to load, we **made a backup version** rather than hope the problem would disappear.

On the day, each person knew what to say, and the teacher asked a useful question about who would maintain the collection points. We had not fully considered that, so we **admitted the limitation** and suggested discussing it with school staff. That answer was more honest than pretending our plan was complete. The project taught me to **listen to different ideas** and **solve problems as a team**. I enjoyed seeing how separate pieces of work could **come together** when we **kept a common goal in mind**.

After the presentation, we kept the slides and notes in a shared folder so each of us could review the feedback. Our idea needed more thought, but the process had strengthened our teamwork. I would happily work with them again on a project with a clearer, manageable scope.
